item.title: Mamdani launches fast-track housing-court push, says landlords unable to comply ‘should not be a landlord’
item.description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced New York City's Unified Court System will fast-track emergency housing court cases involving vacate orders and violations.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Tuesday the debut of the city's new Unified Court System, a mechanism to fast-track emergency cases in New York City Housing Court.

"I am proud to announce that the Unified Court System will now fast-track emergency housing court cases where the health, safety and well-being of New Yorkers is at risk," Mamdani said during a Tuesday news conference.

The new system will reduce the time tenants face to have emergency hearings on potential negligence from landlords, Mamdani explained.

"This fast track will accelerate the cases that are both the most egregious and the most complex. Cases where at least one third of units in a building are subject to an open vacate order. Where families have been forced from their homes. Cases where at least one third of the units have an open and immediately hazardous violation for essential services," he announced.

MANHATTAN BUILDING STABILIZED, SOME EVACUATIONS LIFTED AFTER COLLAPSE FEARED

In cases of "persistent and extreme negligence" where tenants request entirely new building management, judges will require parties to return to court "within five days after service is completed," Mamdani announced.

NYC RENT BOARD DISSENTER WARNS MAMDANI-BACKED FREEZE COULD HURT AFFORDABLE HOUSING OVER TIME: 'SLOW BURN'

When asked how his office would differentiate between a landlord who was persistently negligent and one who simply couldn't afford to keep up with the costs of building management, Mamdani did not hold back.

"We're talking about cases where a third of the building is facing some kind of a serious violation. Cases where we have elevators broken down," he started.

MAMDANI RIPPED OVER 'FREAK SHOW' NEWS CONFERENCE WHERE EVICTION WAS DECLARED A FORM OF 'VIOLENCE'

"When it comes to the law, everyone has to follow it. And for far too long that has somehow not been understood when it comes to housing in our city. If a landlord is not able to follow the law, then they should not be a landlord of that property," he replied.

When asked about how to enforce any violators who might not appear to Housing Court after the five-day window, Mamdani said, "There is still a lot of work to follow through on."

Fox News Digital contacted the mayor's office for further comment.

item.title: The 2026 NFL season hasn't even started yet and the Jacksonville Jaguars are already taking a massive L
item.description: The Jacksonville Jaguars' new NFL Rivalry uniforms feature spotted pants and clashing colors that are already catching serious heat from fans online.
item.content:encoded:
I tend to talk a lot about college football uniforms more than NFL uniforms, but that all changed Tuesday morning.

The NFL rolled out their "Rivalry" series of uniforms for all eight teams from the NFC North and AFC South, and by and large, they did a pretty nice job.

The league partnered with Nike to deliver some uniforms that feature a good bit of franchise history and community pride stitched into each team's garments, and I have to say I'm a fan of the overall concept.

CINCINNATI REDS DEBUT CITY CONNECT UNIFORMS AND THEY ARE AN ABOMINATION

I've always been a bigger fan of college uniforms and felt the NFL threads were a bit too "corporate" and "samey" for my liking, but almost all of these are sweet looking alternate kits.

All of them except for one team, that is.

JACKSONVILLE JAGUARS SET AT 8.5 WIN TOTAL AFTER SURPRISING 13-4 SEASON AND WILD CARD LOSS TO BUFFALO

The Jacksonville Jaguars, being an AFC South team, were included in the "Rivalry" uniform rollout, and if I'm being blunt, they massively swung and missed their intended target with these monstrosities.

Okay, let's start with the positives. At least they aren't the "Color Rush Thursday" mustard uniforms the Jags wore back in the late 2010s.

Well, that's about the only positive I can find, so let's dive in, shall we?

This is way too busy for my liking. The helmet, jersey and socks, and pants all being different colors is murder on my eyes. It looks like a 13-year-old kid customized Jacksonville's uniforms in Madden and picked the most garish combinations possible.

Why didn't they go with a black helmet like the good old days?

Or, if they wanted to do the teal lids, at least get a matching jersey and make the pants white.

And, oh Lord, the pants!

You might not be able to tell, but if you look closely enough on the graphic, those are indeed, spotted pants.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

You know, like a jaguar?

People like to rag on another team from the Sunshine State, the Florida Gators, for their "Gator Skin" jerseys, and rightly so. But these pants are just as egregious and deserve just as much flak.

And believe me, they are catching some heat from fans on social media.

The season hasn't even started yet, and the Jags are already taking L's all over the place.

On the bright side, if Trevor Lawrence throws for 400 yards and three touchdowns while wearing these and Jacksonville wins their division this year, everyone will look back fondly on these uniforms a few decades from now.

Time heals all wounds. Hell, just look at how popular the "Creamsicle" jerseys are in Tampa.

As Marty McFly would say, "I guess you aren't ready for that. But your kids are gonna love it."

item.title: NYC mom survives neck-slash attack on hiking trip in Arizona: 'I can’t die like this'
item.description: Ring camera footage captures New York City mother Alexis Rowan fighting for her life after a stranger slashed her neck on an Arizona birthday hike.
item.content:encoded:
A birthday hiking trip of a lifetime wound up being a death-defying fight for her life for a New York City mother of two, leaving her neck slashed, her hand stabbed, as well as physical and emotional scars that left 13 stitches and a nightmare that will never be forgotten.

Alexis Rowan, 27, survived the northern Arizona mountain-hike attack only because of screams that were heard by a woman in a nearby home, forcing the suspect to flee, harrowing doorbell camera footage showed.

"I was like, oh my God, my neck: I can't die like this, this is not the way," Alexis Rowan told WABC after returning to New York City after last week's ordeal on a tourist mountain hike in Arizona. "I have my kids to go home to."

NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING'

Graphic photos shared by the New York Post showed the deep slash left on her neck and the 10 stitches that closed it, along with three more from being stabbed in the hand.

She never wants "to look at another mountain again," she told the Post, while the lasting scar will remind her of the horror with every look in the mirror.

On the Wednesday, Aug. 19, hike at the Havasupai Indian Reservation – just one day after her 27th birthday – Alexis was left briefly behind a friend when the suspect approached. The suspect, identified as Taylor Nardo Paya, 29, is a Havasupai tribe member with a rap sheet that included a guilty plea to assault, according to FOX 10 Phoenix.

GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL

"It was the first person that I've seen in the village, and I said, 'Hey, excuse me, is that the gift shop?'" Rowan told WABC in one of the few interviews she granted. Fox News Digital reached out to her and her mother for an interview, but they have yet to respond.

"I kept walking, I went to go in and that's when he just came up from behind," she continued, "and as soon as I felt my neck, I'm like, 'Oh my God, I'm going to die.'"

Footage showed Rowan fighting for her life as she was dragged by the hair from the ground – with her screams finally bringing a woman to open the door and causing the suspect to flee. The video obtained by Fox News Digital did not have the sound of the screams, but they were key to the suspect fleeing, according to reports.

REPEAT OFFENDER ACCUSED OF COLLEGE STUDENT’S MURDER WAS KNOWN ‘THREAT’ AFTER PRIOR ARREST: VICTIM’S MOM

"I'm just so grateful for the woman that opened the door that heard her screams; it's something you can never unhear," Tricia Rowan, Alexis' mother, told WABC of the "angel sent from heaven" woman who opened the door to help.

"She's a fighter. She fought to make sure she's coming home to her babies, and she's my baby. So I'm so glad she made it," Tricia Rowan said. "He picked the wrong one. My daughter is a fighter, she is a warrior. She wasn’t going to take it."

SENATOR TIM SHEEHY: SOFT-ON-CRIME JUDGES NEED CONSEQUENCES. THE JAIL ACT DELIVERS

Alexis Rowan told the Post she was "mentally aware" of the "danger" after her initial interaction with Paya.

"My gut instinct was like, ‘This is not OK. I’m not OK,’" she said, adding that the "next person may not be as strong, may not be prepared mentally that someone is going to attack them or able to put them in danger."

Reservation police located Paya the following day by pinging Rowan’s phone, which prosecutors say he allegedly stole after it fell from one of her backpacks.

WOMAN ALLEGEDLY CHOKED SUBWAY RIDER, YELLED ANTISEMITIC REMARKS IN ATTACK CAUGHT ON VIDEO: POLICE

He was arrested and later taken into federal custody because the alleged attack occurred on tribal land, according to reports. Video obtained by Fox News Digital showed Paya being cuffed and taken away on a golf cart by federal police before another video showed him in an orange jumpsuit being perp-walked to a helicopter.

Paya faces a federal assault with a deadly weapon charge, according to FOX 10. Court records show Paya pleaded guilty in 2016 to robbing and assaulting another woman in a 2015 attack, for which he received a five-year prison sentence and was ordered to undergo sex offender treatment and counseling.

The victim's mother wants to see the perpetrator locked up indefinitely.

"People are evil," she told the Post, calling him "a threat to society" and someone "you cannot rehabilitate."

"There is no place on earth that they belong," she added, "other than behind bars like an animal in a cage because they’re predators and they prey on innocent victims."

item.title: Mystery trio in headlamps and overalls emerges from Manhattan manhole, prompting NYPD probe
item.description: The NYPD is reviewing surveillance video after three people in overalls and headlamps were caught emerging from a Manhattan manhole near Penn Station.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Police Department is investigating after video showing three people in overalls and headlamps emerging from a Manhattan manhole went viral on social media.

The NYPD confirmed to Fox News Digital that the incident occurred on Aug. 18 at 4:19 a.m. on the southeast corner of 32nd Street and Seventh Avenue, which is near Penn Station.

No arrests have been made in this case, but police said they are reviewing surveillance video.

NYPD detectives told WABC that they believe many of the people who have been caught on camera doing this are migrants searching for valuables in the sewers.

WOMAN DIES AFTER PLUNGING INTO UNCOVERED MANHOLE OUTSIDE LUXURY STORES

Detectives said a scavenger culture exists in nations like Venezuela.

City officials have said that sneaking into manholes is both illegal and "extremely dangerous."

NYPD INVESTIGATING AFTER SURVEILLANCE VIDEO CAPTURES GROUP ENTERING SEWERS THROUGH MANHOLES

"DEP has inspected the sewers at the location, and our infrastructure is safe. DEP works closely with our public safety partners to help ensure the safety and security of critical infrastructure throughout New York City," the city's Department of Environmental Protection said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

The statement continued: "Entering the sewer system is both illegal and extremely dangerous. Sewers can contain numerous hazards, including noxious and potentially deadly gases, unstable surfaces, flooding risks, and confined spaces. For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole, or outfall."

New York City's sewer system is made up of an elaborate network of more than 7,400 miles of wastewater and stormwater pipes, parts of which date back to the 1800s.

In June, The Associated Press reported on three separate instances of people exiting manholes in Queens and the Williamsburg and Gravesend neighborhoods of Brooklyn.

Many of them were wearing headlamps and were carrying shovels or other tools when they were caught on video.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Antisemitic streamer finally makes Dem leader snap with rare rebuke: ‘Malicious’
item.description: House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries calls Hasan Piker's claim that Jewish Americans invite violence against themselves dangerous and antisemitic.
item.content:encoded:
House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York is slamming comments from Hasan Piker after the far-left controversial online streamer suggested that Jewish Americans were inviting violence against themselves over their support for Israel.

"The malicious claim that American Jews are inviting violence against themselves is dangerous and antisemitic," Jeffries charged in a social media post. And he added in a CNN interview on Tuesday that Piker's comments were "malicious" and "should not be tolerated by anyone in the public square."

While Jeffries became the highest-ranking congressional Democrat to fire back at Piker, the criticism from the top Democrat in the U.S. House comes after he has largely stayed silent on the far-left insurgency, backed in part by Piker, that's gripped his party this election cycle.

Jeffries spoke out after Piker, on his stream last week, featured an image of state Sen. Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee in Michigan's 11th Congressional District. Moss, who is Jewish, has said that people are sharing a fake audio clip of him claiming that his entire reason for running for Congress is to make sure that America continues to support Israel.

EL-SAYED TRIES TO DISTANCE HIMSELF FROM HASAN PIKER AFTER LATEST FIRESTORM

"If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker warned.

Piker, who has over three million online followers, has repeatedly stood by his numerous past comments slamming Israel over its ongoing war against Hamas in Gaza.

Jeffries emphasized in his social media post, "There is zero justification for threats against the safety of our Jewish brothers and sisters at a moment of rising hate. We will fight the cancer of antisemitism with the fierce urgency of now."

ABDUL EL-SAYED FACES OFF WTIH FOX NEWS' JESSE WATTERS IN PRIMETIME

Piker's comments were also blasted by Democratic Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., who charged that Piker is "a hack who thrives on hate."

Rep. Susie Lee, D-Nev., took to X to write, "Claims that American Jews are responsible for the violence being committed against their communities are unacceptable and cannot be tolerated. It’s dangerous and antisemitic."

"We must stand up to the scourge of antisemitism wherever it rears its ugly head," Lee added.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., praised Jeffries' pushback against Piker.

In an interview on Fox News' "America's Newsroom," Gottheimer called Piker's comments something "right out of the Nazi playbook."

Gottheimer, who is Jewish and a strong supporter of Israel, emphasized, "This is a call for violence against Jews,"

He was also critical of Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan.

DEMOCRATS 'WHO NEVER VOTED REPUBLICAN' BACKING THIS GOP SENATE NOMINEE

El-Sayed, who is facing off against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in battleground Michigan in a high-stakes Senate showdown, on Monday tried to put some distance between himself and Piker, who is a top supporter.

"I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople," El-Sayed said in a statement.

Gottheimer said that El-Sayed insufficiently pushed back against Piker: "El-Sayed's response was pathetic,"

"No Democratic members should allow Piker anywhere near them on the campaign trail," Gottheimer argued.

Piker endorsed El-Sayed for the Democratic nomination and appeared at some of the candidate's campaign events including a primary night party earlier this month in Detroit, Michigan.

Piker's latest comments were blasted by a growing number of Republicans since they grabbed attention this past weekend, including Rogers, who took aim at both Piker and El-Sayed in a social media post.

"More calls for violence coming out of the El-Sayed campaign," Rogers said on Sunday. And he claimed, "Here is his running mate, Hasan Piker, saying that if AMERICAN JEWS support Israel, they will be violently targeted because of it."

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Rogers, who is making a major push to court Democrats in Michigan, added, "Absolutely DISGUSTING. If Abdul El-Sayed had any courage at all, he would call this out and disavow Hasan Piker once and for all. We’re waiting, Abdul…"

El-Sayed, in his Monday statement, wrote, "I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past."

"My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters. Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk," he added.

WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM RACES SHOW

A former Wayne County Health Department director, El-Sayed, if elected in November, would make history as the nation's first Muslim senator. The epidemiologist who unsuccessfully ran for governor as an insurgent candidate in 2018 has made support for Medicare for all a major component of his campaign and has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

El-Sayed used the word "bloodthirsty" to characterize Israel's military moves in Gaza in an MS NOW interview this month and accused Israeli leadership of genocide against Palestinians. He has argued against unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel, as have other progressive politicians. And El-Sayed has repeatedly declined to directly answer whether Israel has the right to exist.

But El-Sayed has also repeatedly stated that he stands "in solidarity with my Jewish sisters and brothers" to "condemn antisemitism."

item.title: Former TOPGUN pilot analyzes Marine Corps pilot's eerie calm after emergency F-18 ejection
item.description: Former TOPGUN pilot Matthew Buckley explains the violent forces of ejection and why Marine Corps Maj. Jackson Simon appeared so calm after his F-18 crash.
item.content:encoded:
Former TOPGUN pilot Matthew "Whiz" Buckley told Fox News Digital that the recent crash of a Marine Corps F-18 in Washington state — and the pilot's split-second decision to eject — highlights both the violence of the maneuver and how the ensuing shock can leave an aviator feeling eerily calm.

On June 13, 2026, Marine Corps Maj. Jackson Simon emerged from a wooded area with a bloodied face and walked down the road toward a Yakima County sheriff’s deputy, whose bodycam captured the pilot appearing remarkably composed.

"I'm a little frazzled," was about as close as Simon came to expressing fear after his F-18 Hornet crashed into the forest and sparked a small wildfire near Rimrock Lake.

Buckley, who flew F-18 Hornets during his 15-year career in the U.S. Navy, said Simon was likely experiencing a combination of shock, an adrenaline letdown and the effects of training that teaches pilots to compartmentalize under pressure.

EIGHT BELIEVED DEAD AFTER B-52 CRASHES SHORTLY AFTER TAKEOFF FROM EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE

"If anything's going wrong, we focus on the task. Everything else goes away," Buckley told Fox News Digital. "That was the most violent thing that ever happened to that Marine in his entire life."

Buckley served as a pilot in the Navy from 1991 to 2006 and said he was fortunate never to have ejected from an aircraft. The experience can have a devastating toll on the human body.

"Some folks don't go back to flying status. I mean, you can lose a couple inches in height. Your spine compresses. Some people get shorter," Buckley said.

A meta-analysis of more than a dozen studies looking at 1,710 military aircrew ejections found a pooled mortality rate of 10.5%, while 29.8% suffered major injuries. The studies were published between 1971 and 2019.

ARMY IDENTIFIES 2 PILOTS KILLED IN APACHE HELICOPTER CRASH NEAR FORT HOOD DURING TRAINING EXERCISE

"When you pull that handle, you have two choices: die or maybe live. And I said 'maybe live' because it's incredibly violent. I think the average ejection seat is like 10 to 20 G's of force," Buckley added. "Most folks don't even remember the ejection. They remember pulling the handle and then waking up in their parachute."

Buckley said the pilot's body positioning before the ejection is extremely important in preventing potentially life-threatening injuries. For example, if their arm is extended away from their body, the sudden wind blast could cause it to be "ripped out of the socket."

There's also a phenomenon called "seat slap," which occurs if the pilot does not have their legs flush with the seat prior to ejecting.

"If you look at an ejection seat in a fighter jet, it's rock hard. We're not sitting on a cushion," he said. "If your legs aren't flat on the seat, it could break both of your legs and now you bleed out and die."

US NAVY IDENTIFIES SAILOR LOST IN ARABIAN SEA AFTER HELICOPTER'S EMERGENCY WATER LANDING

In some instances, pilots who find themselves in trouble have time to slow their aircraft and perform a controlled ejection, which can reduce the forces involved, Buckley said.

Based on video of the crash, Simon’s plane was traveling at a high rate of speed before it struck the trees and exploded, likely leaving little opportunity for a controlled ejection.

Simon had been performing low-flying maneuvers while spectators on the ground watched, according to KIRO 7. After that, his plane reportedly clipped some power lines, which led to it going down.

The Marine Corps has not publicly confirmed that Simon’s F-18 struck power lines before the crash and has said the cause of the mishap remains under investigation.

UNITED AIRLINES JET FLEW TOO LOW AND TOO SLOW BEFORE STRIKING LIGHT POLE AND TRUCK NEAR NEWARK AIRPORT: NTSB

According to Buckley, this "clearly" wasn't supposed to happen.

"We have minimum altitude restrictions. And there ain't no 500-foot trees, right? So I don't know what they were doing. It doesn't sound like from his initial statement that there was anything wrong with the airplane. So that's usually not a good sign," Buckley said.

Buckley then speculated about what may have been going through Simon’s mind before the crash.

"It looked like a beautiful day. People out on a lake. 'Hey, there's some people down there on the lake. Why don't we go show them what their tax money is [for]? You know, America.' I hope it wasn't something like that," he said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the third Marine Aircraft Wing, the West Coast-based Marine aviation unit to which Simon’s aircraft was assigned.

Buckley said Simon will likely go before a review board that will evaluate his actions surrounding the crash. At the conclusion of the process, the board can recommend what should happen to an aviator’s flight status.

If he's found to be at fault, Simon could lose his "wings" or he could be allowed to continue flying, just under what Buckley described as "double secret probation."

"I don't know what the board's gonna do, but it'll come out. It should because...this is a $60 to $65 million Hornet. We deserve to know what happened," he added.

item.title: New Padres owner Kwanza Jones puts on a performance for the ages at introductory presser
item.description: Kwanza Jones broke into a spirited chant about winning it all during her introduction as a new San Diego Padres owner after the $3.9 billion sale.
item.content:encoded:
As a singer and songwriter, Kwanza Jones knows a thing or two about putting on a performance, and she made sure to show off those abilities as she was introduced as a new owner of the San Diego Padres.

Jones, along with her husband, Jose E. Feliciano, took over ownership of the Padres in a $3.9 billion sale from John Seidler and his family earlier this month. The pair were introduced to the media in San Diego on Monday, and it's safe to assume that Jones is rather excited about the new, incredibly expensive endeavor in Major League Baseball.

"We gonna win. We gonna win. We’re going to win, win it all," Jones shouted while offering up some hand gestures as well. "We hope it’s sooner rather than later."

SAN DIEGO PADRES STAR MANNY MACHADO IS WRONG TO COMPLAIN ABOUT MODERN MAJOR LEAGUE BASEBALL

Jones also stood up at one point during the news conference and took a picture of the gathered media with her phone.

Padres fans are hopeful that sooner rather than later part comes to fruition, especially considering that they've been waiting forever to see San Diego win a World Series.

The Padres have played in the World Series twice in franchise history, most recently in 1998, but have never hoisted the Commissioner's Trophy.

PRIVATE EQUITY COMPANY APOLLO AGREES TO FINANCE DEAL WITH NEW YORK YANKEES ORGANIZATION FOR $2.6 BILLION

Feliciano is an investor and the co-founder and managing partner of the investment firm called Clearlake Capital, the 12th largest private equity firm in the world. Forbes reports that his net worth is $3.9 billion.

Feliciano is not new to the sports owner's world, as Clearlake co-led a group of investors in an acquisition of Chelsea in the Premier League in May 2022.

Jones and Feliciano could be in store to witness postseason baseball in San Diego this year, with the Padres currently holding onto the third Wild Card spot in the National League with a record of 71-61.

The Padres currently hold a two-game lead over the Arizona Diamondbacks in the Wild Card race with 30 regular-season games to go.

item.title: Formula 1 champ Max Verstappen set to take on 100 go-karters in wild made-for-TV stunt
item.description: Max Verstappen will race against 100 go-karters on a purpose-built track at Silverstone in a made-for-TV event airing on ESPN and on Disney+.
item.content:encoded:
If you've ever wondered what it would be like to turn one of the best Formula 1 drivers of all-time loose on a karting track with 100 mere mortals, we're going to find out.

It was announced that Red Bull's four-time champion Max Verstappen — fresh off a rough weekend in which he crashed out of his home race on the opening lap — will take on scores of karters in a special, made-for-TV event called "Max vs 100."

It will take place on a purpose-built karting track at Silverstone — site of the British Grand Prix — and will be broadcast on ESPN and streamed on Disney+.

This will be wild.

First of all, I'm a sucker for made-for-TV stunts. Motorcycle jumps, tightrope walks, whatever David Blaine feels like doing (which is usually hanging upside down or sitting in a chunk of ice for a few days), I'm in.

EVEL KNIEVEL'S MOST LEGENDARY STUNTS RETOLD IN EXCLUSIVE NEW FOX NATION DOCUMENTARY

While this doesn't have the danger factor of Evel Knievel sending it over the fountain at Caesars Palace, it will be a display of just how good the Dutchman is behind the wheel of anything.

I don't think it's a matter of whether Max Verstappen can overtake go-karters; it's how long it will take him to do it.

Like most F1 drivers, Verstappen started his racing career on karts, so he'll have to reach into his old bag of tricks.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

"In go-karts you learn all the basics: starts, defending, overtaking," he said in a statement, per Motorsport. "Of course, I spent a long period of my life go-karting, so it's always nice to return. It’s about understanding the grip of the go-kart. I've done so many years in go-karting that you quite naturally get back into things."

I'm curious to see how hard the karters defend against him. On one hand, it would be cool to say you made it hard for a driver of Verstappen's caliber to get past you, but you don't want to be the guy who causes a crash by moving under braking or not leaving enough space through a corner.

Don't. Be. That. Guy.

item.title: ICE lodges detainer for illegal immigrant with lengthy rap sheet after alleged jealousy-fueled killing
item.description: ON FOX: Federal immigration officials lodged an ice detainer for a Cuban citizen with drug trafficking convictions charged with second-degree murder.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Federal immigration officials are asking authorities in the Miami area to honor a detainer request for an illegal immigrant with a lengthy criminal history who is now charged with fatally shooting a man on the street in an alleged act of jealousy.

William Serrano Domenech, 49, is being held in a Miami-Dade County jail in connection with the Aug. 17 murder of 42-year-old Raul Aballe, the Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday.

"He has a rap sheet a mile long, with prior convictions in Florida and Michigan for drug trafficking and illegal possession of a firearm, as well as prior arrests in New Mexico and Tennessee for aggravated assault, theft, and resisting arrest," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "This dangerous criminal should have never been in our country, and had it not been for the Biden Administration releasing him from ICE custody in 2023, Raul Aballe would still be alive."

EXCLUSIVE: DHS SEEKS CUSTODY OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER TRUMP DEPORTATION, BIDEN RELEASE

Domenech, a Cuban citizen, was "socializing with the witness" on the evening of the slaying when Aballe appeared and the pair began arguing, authorities said. The dispute turned physical when Domenech started punching and slapping Aballe, authorities said.

Domenech allegedly pulled a gun out of a fanny pack and opened fire, striking Aballe in the stomach. Aballe was taken to a hospital where he later died.

ICE LODGES DETAINER ON SALVADORAN NATIONAL, 18, ACCUSED OF 2 FATAL SHOOTINGS IN HOUSTON

Domenech allegedly fled the scene, but he was arrested the next day. He allegedly admitted to the killing and said he was jealous of Aballe's relationship with the witness, according to authorities.

The witness reportedly told investigators that Aballe was not armed and didn't initiate the fight.

HOW A NONCITIZEN SUSPECTED KILLER GOT CAUGHT AND RELEASED BY NEWSOM-APPOINTED JUDGE: TIMELINE

Domenech is charged with second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged a detainer with Miami-Dade authorities the day after Domenech's arrest.

His criminal history spans at least four states for a litany of offenses, DHS said. That includes a conviction for a weapons offense and arrests on charges of vehicle theft, burglary, driving without a license, and driving with a suspended license in Florida, as well as prior arrests on charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, false imprisonment, and bribery of a witness in New Mexico.

HUNDREDS OF JAILED ILLEGAL ALIENS RELEASED BACK ONTO BLUE-STATE STREETS DESPITE ICE DETAINERS, RECORDS SHOW

In addition, Domenech has prior arrests for unlawful possession of a weapon, resisting arrest, and theft in Tennessee, and convictions for possession with intent to distribute five grams or more of cocaine, possession with intent to distribute an unknown quantity of marijuana, possession of firearms in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, possession of a firearm by an illegal alien, and felon in possession of a firearm in Michigan, authorities said.

Domenech allegedly told authorities he entered the United States through Florida in 1995. A deportation order was issued by a judge in 2002.

ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH BRUTAL SLAYING ONE DAY AFTER CALIFORNIA JUDGE RELEASED HIM: DHS

However, when ICE took him into custody in 2023, he was released back onto the streets by the Biden administration, DHS said.

"ICE has lodged a detainer and will work with our partners in Florida to ensure that this killer is never again allowed back onto our streets," Mullin said.

item.title: Georgia sheriff seizes 1,800 pounds of suspected black-market marijuana shipped from California
item.description: A 1,800-pound black market marijuana shipment from Sacramento, California, was intercepted in Georgia, reportedly bound for Atlanta and Orlando.
item.content:encoded:
A massive shipment of 1,800 pounds of suspected black-market marijuana from California was intercepted in Georgia on Tuesday, with authorities saying the drugs were destined for Atlanta and Orlando.

The shipment originated in Sacramento, where recreational marijuana is legal, according to the Butts County Sheriff’s Office. Sheriff Gary Long said about half of the marijuana was bound for Atlanta, while the rest was headed to Orlando.

The sheriff’s office did not say where or how the shipment was intercepted, whether anyone was arrested or whether charges were filed.

NY TIMES WALKS BACK STANCE ON MARIJUANA LEGALIZATION, ADMITS LOOSENING OF POLICIES HAS MADE COUNTRY WORSE OFF

Long used the seizure to make his case that legalizing marijuana does not eliminate illegal sales.

"But here is the reality: the black market isn't going away," Long said in a press release announcing the seizure.

Marijuana laws vary among the three states connected to the shipment. California allows recreational marijuana, while Georgia and Florida allow marijuana only for certain medical uses.

"The illegal marijuana trade does not stop at the state line," Long said.

Long said Mexican drug-trafficking organizations and other criminal groups continue to move large amounts of marijuana across state lines. The sheriff’s office did not say the shipment seized Tuesday was connected to a cartel or any other criminal organization.

The sheriff also argued that illegal sellers can undercut licensed marijuana businesses because they don't pay taxes or licensing fees or have to follow testing and other regulatory requirements.

"As long as there is demand and money to be made, illegal dealers will continue to operate," Long said.

AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING

Long urged Georgia lawmakers to look closely at what has happened in states that have legalized marijuana before making changes to Georgia's laws.

He pointed to California, which has changed its cannabis tax and regulatory system while continuing to fight illegal marijuana sales. He also cited past ballot initiatives filed in Colorado seeking to repeal constitutional provisions that legalized recreational marijuana, though those efforts did not reverse legalization.

"That should be a warning to Georgia," Long said. "We should learn from the experiences of states that have already gone down this road instead of repeating the same mistakes and then spending years trying to fix them."

Long said his statement was not meant to settle the question of whether marijuana should be legal. Instead, he argued that lawmakers need to consider how illegal sales and trafficking would fit into any changes to Georgia law.

"Georgia, let's get it right the first time," Long said.

item.title: Google Docs password leak reveals a costly security mistake
item.description: A contractor stored credentials in a Google Doc set to "Anyone with the link," and Google Search autocomplete eventually surfaced the password string.
item.content:encoded:
Passwords have a way of ending up in places they were never meant to live. Sometimes convenience wins in the moment, and security becomes tomorrow's problem. One company learned that lesson after a contractor stored credentials in a Google Doc so they could access them from different devices.

Then something happened that should make anyone who uses Google Docs take a closer look at their sharing settings. A developer searching the company's domain on Google saw one of its staging hostnames appear in autocomplete alongside what looked like a credential string. The company investigated and found a Google Docs URL that anyone with the link could access.

That's a rough way to discover that a password has traveled much farther than you intended. Here's how the exposure happened, what Google says about Docs privacy and the simple steps you can take to keep your own passwords and shared files safer.

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.

WORLD PASSWORD DAY: CHECK IF YOUR PASSWORDS ARE SAFE

The story was reported by The Register and comes from Siim Kostabi, co-founder of Pageloot, a company that provides QR codes for businesses. Kostabi said his company brought in an outside contractor to help with back-end API integrations. The contractor had credentials for the company's staging environment, which is essentially a test version of its system.

The contractor wanted easy access to those credentials from multiple devices. So they put the information into a Google Doc and set the document so anyone with the link could view it. Later, a Pageloot developer was working on an unrelated problem and typed the company's domain into Google Search. Autocomplete surfaced one of the staging hostnames followed by what appeared to be a credential string.

The team checked and found the accessible Google Docs URL. The Register reported that Google Search had indexed the document and offered information from it as a search suggestion. Pageloot quickly cut off the contractor's access and rotated the exposed credentials. The company also adopted a rule against storing passwords in Google Docs, Slack or Notion and other collaboration tools.

Before you start worrying that every Google Doc you have ever created could suddenly appear in a search, there is an important piece of context. Google told CyberGuy that Google Docs are restricted by default. The person who creates the document controls how it gets shared.

Google's current Drive guidance says Restricted means only people with access can open a file. If you select Anyone with the link, anyone who gets that link can use the file without signing in to a Google Account. Google separately lists a Public setting, when available, that allows anyone to find the file through Google Search.

Google also told CyberGuy that a link to a publicly shared Doc may be indexed if someone posts that link somewhere public where a search engine crawler can find it. The Register says the Pageloot document eventually surfaced through Google Search autocomplete. However, the report does not explain how Google first discovered the Docs URL. For the rest of us, the useful lesson is simple: pay attention to the sharing setting before putting anything sensitive in a cloud document.

Kostabi also described a separate incident involving one of Pageloot's customers. The midsize retailer discovered that its QR codes had started sending shoppers to a competitor's website.

According to Kostabi, the company investigated and found that a former employee's credentials had never been revoked. He said the former employee used that lingering access to redirect the retailer's URLs. That mistake carries a very familiar lesson.

When someone no longer needs access to an account or shared file, their access should go away too. That applies at work, but it can also apply at home. Maybe you once shared a financial document with an accountant. Perhaps an old household file still includes someone who no longer needs it. Shared access can be easy to forget because the file quietly remains in Google Drive.

WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE

You do not have to run a business to learn something from this story. Plenty of people use Google Docs and Drive to keep household information, travel plans or tax documents and other details they want available across devices.

The danger comes when sensitive information lands in a file with broader access than you realize. A Google Doc can feel private because you remember sending the link to only one person. What really counts is who currently has permission to open it and what the General access setting says. That makes this a good time to check the files you would least want a stranger opening.

A few small changes can reduce the chance that an old shared file or exposed password turns into a much bigger security problem.

If you have passwords sitting in a Google Doc right now, move them to a reputable password manager. Password managers are designed to securely store logins and make them available across your devices. They can also help you create unique passwords instead of reusing the same one. Check out the best expert-reviewed password managers of 2026 at Cyberguy.com for options and what to look for. After moving a password, delete it from the document. If other people may have had access to the file, change that password too.

Start with documents containing financial information or account details.

On a computer:

Google says switching General access to Restricted means only people with access can open the file.

On iPhone, iPad or Android:

This setting can be handy when you need to share something quickly. However, anyone who gets the link can access the file without signing in to a Google Account. That link can also get forwarded or copied somewhere you never expected. For sensitive documents, share the file directly with specific people instead.

Open the sharing settings on important files and scan the list of people who can still get in. If someone no longer needs access, remove them. This is especially worth doing after you finish working with a contractor or service provider. At home, the same idea applies when you have shared a document temporarily and the reason for sharing it has passed.

Changing a Google Doc from broad access to Restricted helps close the door, but it cannot undo exposure that may have already happened. If a password was sitting in a document other people could access, change it. Then check the account's recent login or security activity for anything you do not recognize.

Two-factor authentication adds another step when someone tries to sign in to your account. That can help protect you if a password gets stolen. CyberGuy's guide to multifactor authentication apps can help you strengthen accounts that support this added protection.

Strong antivirus software adds another layer of protection on your computer and phone. It cannot fix a Google Doc with the wrong sharing setting. However, it can help detect malicious downloads, phishing attempts and other threats that may follow if criminals get hold of your login information. Keep your security software updated and make sure real-time protection stays turned on. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Identity theft protection makes the most sense when an exposed document contained more than a password. For example, you may want extra monitoring if someone gained access to your Social Security number, financial account information or other highly sensitive personal data. Identity theft protection services can watch for signs that your information is being misused. Some also alert you to suspicious activity tied to your identity. If the exposure involved only one account password, changing that password and securing the account may be enough. The level of protection you need depends on what information was actually exposed. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

You probably have old Google Drive files you have not opened in months or even years. Spend a few minutes checking the sharing settings on documents containing sensitive information. You may find an old permission you completely forgot about. For more ways to lock down cloud files, see our guide on protecting sensitive documents and controlling file access.

Google also addressed a separate privacy question with CyberGuy. The company told us that it does not use private Workspace content, including Drive and Docs, to train its foundational AI models such as Gemini. Google's published Workspace guidance likewise says Workspace data isn’t used to train or improve the underlying generative AI models that power Gemini, Search and other systems outside Workspace without permission. That issue is separate from what happened in the Pageloot story. This case centered on how the document was shared and how credentials were handled.

FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK

What gets me about this story is how ordinary the original decision probably felt. Someone needed a password on more than one device and chose an easy place to put it. That shortcut eventually left company credentials where Google Search autocomplete could surface them. The second incident carries another lesson I think all of us can use. Access should have an expiration date. When somebody no longer needs to open one of your files or accounts, remove them. I would also take five minutes today and look at the Google Docs you care about most. Check the people who can open them and look at the General access setting. You may find nothing wrong. Great. But if you uncover an old shared link or a person who should no longer have access, you will be glad you looked before somebody else did.

When was the last time you checked who can still open the Google Docs and Drive files you've shared over the years? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: Second lady Usha Vance fires back at pointed jab from Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed
item.description: Usha Vance responded to Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's remark that seemingly questioned whether JD Vance's Papaw would have accepted her Indian ethnicity.
item.content:encoded:
PROGRAMMING NOTE: Watch the exclusive interview with second lady Usha Vance Wednesday on "Fox & Friends," starting at 6am ET.

Second lady Usha Vance responded to what critics described as a "racist" dig from Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who appeared to question how Vice President JD Vance’s grandfather would have regarded her.

The exchange began after Vance criticized El-Sayed’s views on Sharia law during a rally in Ohio, arguing the practice would be completely alien to his grandfather, whom he calls his "Papaw."

"He once argued, not too long ago, that criticisms of Sharia law were rooted in White supremacy," Vance said of El-Sayed, the American-born son of Muslim Egyptian immigrants.

VANCE UNLOADS ON EL-SAYED OVER SHARIA REMARKS: ‘THAT’S NOT MY GRANDPA’S DEMOCRATIC PARTY’

"I'd love to go back in time and tell my Papaw that there is a man who claims to stand for working people who says not only should we have Sharia law, but if you criticize it, you're a White supremacist. That's not my Papaw’s Democratic Party, my friends," the vice president continued.

Responding to the vice president’s jab, El-Sayed wrote: "So do we think JD is taking Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no…"

Critics interpreted the remark as an insinuation that Vance’s grandfather would not have accepted Usha because of her Indian heritage.

EL-SAYED UNDER FIRE ONLINE AFTER TAKING AIM AT USHA VANCE, FEMALE TRUMP AIDE IN WEEKEND SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS

"I have to admit, I kind of laughed," Usha Vance told "Fox & Friends" in an exclusive interview set to air Wednesday morning.

"Because yes, I never met JD's Mamaw and Papaw. But I do know and love the children that they raised, his mom, his aunt and uncle. And they have never been anything but incredibly loving."

El-Sayed further addressed the comment in an interview on Saturday.

"The confusing thing about it is that he thinks that there are some people who are more American than others because they can point to their Papaw who was here earlier," he told MS NOW. "And my question to him is simply: Why is it then, how do you look your parents-in-law in the eye and say that somehow they're less American than you are? Because that's what he's implying there."

JD was raised in large part by his grandparents, James and Bonnie Vance, who he calls his "Papaw" and "Mamaw." James died in 1997 and Bonnie died eight years later.

Usha and JD met while attending Yale Law School and married in 2014. Although she never met her husband's late grandparents, the mother of four said her husband’s aunt has become a "second mother" to her.

"His aunt is like a second mother to me," said the second lady. "And so I have to think that if they raised children like that, they would have been loving as well. And I would have really, really, really loved to have met them."

In his 2016 memoir, "Hillbilly Elegy," Vance wrote that one of his "great regrets" was that his grandparents never had the opportunity to meet his wife.

El-Sayed’s campaign did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: Dolly Parton dead at 80
item.description: Dolly Parton, country music legend, has died after months of battling unknown health issues. Her nephew announced the news in a video posted to her Instagram page.
item.content:encoded:
Legendary country singer and songwriter Dolly Parton has died. She was 80. 

Parton died peacefully in Nashville, Tennessee on Tuesday, according to a press release obtained by Fox News Digital. 

Her nephew revealed the news in an Aug. 25 Instagram video. The news comes after Parton spent months battling an unknown health issue.

DOLLY PARTON ADMITS HUSBAND CARL DEAN'S DEATH HAS BEEN 'BIG ADJUSTMENT' AFTER 60-YEAR ROMANCE

"My name is Brin Seaver, son of Cassie Parton, and I’m representing the Parton and Owens family today announcing the passing of my aunt, Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean, Sister, Sis and Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next," he says in the video. "This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality. As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it until now."

"It is an honor, an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness. But sadness lies with us, not with Dolly. Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents and countless others who have watched her and longed to meet her in the heavens."

"I first went on the road with Dolly as a kid, getting a taste of the road life in the early 1980s. Dolly opened doors not just for me, but for her entire family to reach the potential we didn’t even know was possible. Dolly also opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent," Seaver added in the video message. "By her example, we believed that anything is possible. She never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the doors she opened made and changed history."

"My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you," Seaver continued. "She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family whether you liked it or not. Our family and the team she has entrusted with her legacy will work diligently to ensure her spirit will live with us forever. Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy; he farmed the soil, she farmed songs and happiness. Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because, after a life of wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest."

"Rest in peace, Aunt Dolly — Aunt, Granny, Gigi. May God bless Dolly Parton, and may God bless you all. She will always love you."

Born in 1946 in rural Sevier County, Tennessee, Parton grew up in a large, poor family in the Smoky Mountains. She began singing in church as a child, started writing songs at a young age and moved to Nashville after graduating high school to pursue music.

Her breakthrough came as a performer on "The Porter Wagoner Show," where she became a fan favorite before forging a solo path that would establish her as one of country music’s most prolific and influential songwriters.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I’ll always be a country musician because I’m a country girl," she told People in 1975. "My style is my soul and my feelings. I’ll tell the world in my songs what I wouldn’t have told my mother."

Parton’s catalog included enduring hits such as "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "Here You Come Again," "9 to 5" and "I Will Always Love You." The latter song became a global phenomenon again when Whitney Houston recorded it for 1992’s "The Bodyguard."

DOLLY PARTON UNABLE TO WRITE NEW SONGS AFTER LOSING HUSBAND OF NEARLY 60 YEARS

Parton made her feature film debut opposite Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin in 1980’s "9 to 5." Parton later appeared in films including "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas," "Rhinestone," "Steel Magnolias" and "Joyful Noise."

Parton was also known for her decades-long marriage to Carl Dean, who largely stayed out of the public eye during their nearly 60 years together. Dean died in March 2025.

After Dean died at the age of 82, the "Jolene" singer explained why she couldn't get herself to do what she loved: write songs. 

"I can’t afford the luxury of, you know, getting that emotional right now," she said during an appearance on Khloé Kardashian’s podcast, "Khloé in Wonder Land." "There are times like that, things like that, that will stall you a little bit. But I’ll write something else though, if it comes."

"I’m just putting that all on hold," Parton said. 

In November of that same year, the country music legend opened up about her impressive career spanning more than seven decades, got candid about the personal sacrifices she's made throughout the years and explained why she feels like she's "just getting started."

"You know, I have just been going so fast my whole life," Parton told People at the time. "And I just start thinking, ‘How in the world did I even have a life? How did I even get it done?’ I really realized when I was putting this book together just how much I had sacrificed in my life. I never had children, so at least I didn’t have a guilty feeling. I’m thankful that I got to see my dreams come true."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"People say, ‘Well, you’re going to be 80 years old.’ Well, so what? Look at all I’ve done in 80 years. I feel like I’m just getting started," said Parton. "I know that sounds stupid, but unless my health gives way, which right now I seem to be doing fine… I think there’s a lot to be said about age. If you allow yourself to get old, you will. I say, ‘I ain’t got time to get old!’ I ain’t got time to dwell on that. That’s not what I’m thinking about."

Parton has battled various health issues over the past couple of years. 

In May, the country legend announced she was canceling her planned Las Vegas residency, which had already been postponed from 2025 to September 2026 because of health concerns.

Earlier this month, Parton missed a major Dollywood event per doctor's orders. 

"I’m still in Nashville, and I’m sorry about that," Parton told the crowd during a video appearance at the event, according to video shared by the Knoxville News Sentinel.

"I’m supposed to be there in person, like we planned," she continued. "Now I’ve told you before, all my fans, that I have had a few little health issues. And sometimes I get a little dizzy, and I get dehydrated."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"And I’m dehydrated," Parton, who appeared on-screen wearing fairy wings, told the crowd. "And, so, my Nashville doctor clipped my wings, saying, 'You ain’t traveling this week.’"

Parton had previously discussed problems involving kidney stones, saying her immune and digestive systems had gotten "out of whack" and were being treated. 

Beyond her impressive career, Parton built a business empire centered in her home state of Tennessee. Dollywood became one of Tennessee’s most popular attractions, while her charitable work through the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library left an equally lasting mark.

The Imagination Library, which sends free books to children from birth until kindergarten, was inspired by Parton’s father, who never learned to read or write. The program grew into an international literacy initiative and distributed millions of books to families around the world.

At Parton’s request, a small, private service will be held for immediate family.

item.title: GOP's Singer 'very prepared' to oust Dem Moskowitz in toss-up Florida race that could determine House majority
item.description: Scott Singer says Florida's redrawn 25th Congressional District gives Republicans a path to flip Jared Moskowitz's seat in a narrowly divided House.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., a self-described moderate, is facing political headwinds in the race for the newly-redrawn 25th Congressional District in South Florida, as Republican nominee Scott Singer sees a path to pick up a House seat in a narrowly divided Congress.

"We're going to be very prepared to go flip this seat – it is a key targeted seat," Singer told Fox News Digital in an interview Monday.

"This is a key district that may determine the balance of power in the House."

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME

The race is drawing national attention and, potentially, big Democratic dollars to defend the seat in Democrats' pursuit of the majority to attack what House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries just called the "cartel" of President Donald Trump.

"A lot of people in this district and beyond understand what's at stake here," Singer, former Boca Raton mayor, said.

Moskowitz, currently seated in the more Democratic-friendly 23rd District, is – like Singer – Jewish and pro-Israel, but he will have to navigate a tougher Republican-friendly map and fend off the "anti-Israel wing" of the Democratic Party, according to to Singer.

FLORIDA DEMOCRAT SENDS 'CONDOLENCES' TO HASAN PIKER AFTER DEFEATING DSA CHALLENGER IN FLORIDA PRIMARY

"His voting record speaks volumes," Singer said. "Since he's gotten to Congress, he's been locked up with the Democrats on almost every issue."

"This is not the sort of record of bipartisanship he once had. He's been much more partisan because he has to be," Singer claimed. "He has to appeal to a more far-left socialist led Democratic Party if he's going to have any influence. And that's going home to roost in November."

When reached for comment, the two-term Moskowitz stressed he fought off the Democratic Socialists of America's maximum pressure campaign in his primary, while keeping $2 million cash on hand for the general election and expecting "we'll have the national resources" in the fight to keep the seat blue.

"I go after my party all the time and fight within," Moskowitz, who was twice appointed to positions by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis in a show of bipartisanship, told Fox News Digital, noting Singer has been "awfully silent" on social media amid his own vocal defense against the "anti-Israel" political factions.

FROM WASSERMAN SCHULTZ TO GOLDMAN, DEMOCRATIC INCUMBENTS ARE FIGHTING FOR SURVIVAL

"Scott just has talking points, which is why he's the masked singer. You hear a voice behind a mask. He says things to all sorts of people, tells people what they want to hear, but nobody really knows where he stands because he never really takes positions."

The heated rhetoric belies a previously tighter relationship.

"Scott Singer endorsed me when I ran the first time," Moskowitz claimed.

Singer's campaign has denied it was anything more than a personal call to generally express support for a fellow Jewish, pro-Israel politician.

Singer, though, says he is well-positioned in the newly redrawn South Florida district, with a growing GOP voter-registration advantage and Democratic division working against the "quasi-incumbent."

"People are abandoning the Democratic Party because the mainstream Democratic Party of even a few years ago has abandoned them," Singer said. "It's now a socialist-led party and it's sad for America."

"That's why we need to band together and make sure independent voters understand what's at stake," he added. "We can't have people talking about communism or new Democrat-incoming members of the House saying horrific things like that they would wipe their hand on the American flag if they didn't have a napkin. That's today's Democratic Party, unfortunately, and it's not something I want to see."

MOSKOWITZ REJECTS RICK SCOTT'S CLAIMS HE'S 'SCARED TO DEATH' OF SOCIALISTS, BEHOLDEN TO HASAN PIKER

The race is considered to be one of 19 toss-ups in the nation (seats held by four Democrats and 15 Republicans), according to the Cook Political Report.

"It's now about five points more Republican than Democrat, but even since redistricting, there are Republicans who are registering at a higher rate: People in Florida have seen the success of our state and seen the craziness other places, and they're voting more conservative," Singer said.

"And we have a great opportunity to pick off disaffected Democrats who are sick with the socialist lean, especially in our community that has a large number of residents who fled communism, like my family, like wife's family did," he continued. "They understand that bringing socialism and communism into the United States is a terrible idea. That's another reason why we're optimistic about our chances to flip this must-win seat in November."

DESANTIS UNDER PRESSURE AS FLORIDA REDRAW COULD TIP HOUSE BALANCE IN GOP MAP FIGHT

The race also presents an unusual political dynamic: Singer and Moskowitz are both Jewish candidates competing in a district where roughly a quarter of the electorate is Jewish, one of the highest concentrations in the country.

"The anti-Israel wing, which has taken root in the Democratic Party, is doing the convincing for us," Singer said. "Because we've seen a majority of House members would deny arms sales to Israel, our ally during a time of conflict.

"And that's the party, where it is. We've seen three incumbents in the Democratic Party ousted in recent months solely because Israel was the key issue.

"Anti-Israel is winning. It's become the mainstream of the Democratic Party. And longtime Democrats are leaving in droves. Another reason why it's going to be very hard for Democrats in this district to win with 25% Jewish population and people who understand Israel's close and long-standing alliance with the United States. We're going to pick off more of those voters."

5 TAKEAWAYS FROM FLORIDA SENATE PRIMARY: GOP SEN. ASHLEY MOODY WILL FACE DSA'S NIXON

Also, while GOP-leaning, the district is still largely independent. It snakes along South Florida's Atlantic coast through portions of Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade counties, encompassing communities around Delray Beach, Boca Raton, Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood and Miami Beach.

"I was already running under the prior boundaries when it leaned Democratic, but I'm thrilled with the new boundaries because it runs from Miami Beach, where I was born, through Fort Lauderdale where I grew up, through Boca Raton where I served as mayor for eight years," Singer said.

"I have deep ties in this district. It's my whole life. I've lived 40-plus years in this District in all three counties. My opponent doesn't live in the district. I'm not sure he's ever lived in the district. And I think those community ties help when you're trying to represent 750,000-plus people."

Moskowitz lives in nearby Parkland and was born and raised in Coral Springs, which is just west of the newly drawn district, which carved those towns out.

FLA DEM SEN-NOMINEE ANGIE NIXON BACKED ABOLISHING ELECTORAL COLLEGE, RANKED-CHOICE VOTING IN RESURFACED CLIPS

Trump would have carried the territory by roughly nine points in 2024 after Joe Biden would have won it by about five points in 2020, showing just how the district is turning conservative and more favorable to flip.

"Jewish voters don't just have to vote for a Jewish candidate who may be not terrible on Israel ... now you have a pro-Israel, Zionist candidate who's a strong Republican who will vote for the common sense solutions: We need like less regulation, lower taxes, insurance reform and more."

"Independent voters have a choice," he added. "Are we going to continue on tax reform, secure borders, economic improvement... or are we going to go back to what the Democrats would propose, which frankly for the next two years is just impeachment?

"Nothing will get done in Washington," he concluded.

item.title: Dangerous debris washes ashore before beachgoer makes another troubling find
item.description: A Jersey Shore beachgoer says she found more needle plungers and drug paraphernalia the day after Manasquan Beach reopened following a syringe cleanup.
item.content:encoded:
A popular Jersey Shore beach reopened to swimmers after dozens of syringes washed ashore — only for a beachgoer to report finding more concerning debris along the sand the following day.

The syringes and paraphernalia were discovered littered across the sands of Manasquan Beach in Manasquan, along the Jersey Shore, on Saturday.

Officials at the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) said the debris included household waste, including syringes used for at-home insulin injections, according to local outlets.

DANGEROUS WATER WARNINGS HIT TRENDY VACATION SPOT AFTER POWERFUL STORM POUNDS AREA

Mayor Michael Mangan told Fox News Digital the syringes were first discovered Saturday afternoon and were cleaned up and properly cleared away. 

"There was a large amount of additional debris, indicating a garbage spill of some kind, and the incident was localized to the south end beach, along the Manasquan Inlet jetty," Mangan said.

It's believed the debris washed ashore following recent heavy rainfall and sewer overflows, according to local reports citing the NJDEP.

item.title: Pro-life CEO predicts Trump FDA nominee could bring renewed scrutiny to abortion drug risks
item.description: Trump's FDA nominee Heidi Overton could bring renewed scrutiny to mifepristone, says Americans United for Life CEO who calls her a "pro-life" pick.
item.content:encoded:
The chief executive of America's oldest pro-life organization told Fox News Digital that President Donald Trump's FDA nominee, Dr. Heidi Overton, could bring renewed scrutiny to mifepristone, the abortion drug at the center of an ongoing federal safety review.

John Mize, CEO of Americans United for Life (AUL), said he has had five or six conversations with Overton, who is known for her pro-life views. She currently serves as Trump's deputy assistant for domestic policy.

"I think she's going to bring objectivity to the issue of mifepristone in a way that will expose this drug for the damage it causes women," Mize said in an interview on Friday, adding that his organization is "optimistic" that Overton will be a "pro-life FDA commissioner."

Overton's nomination comes just weeks after an 18-year-old woman in North Carolina was accused of using mifepristone and misoprostol to terminate a pregnancy at 31 weeks, well beyond mifepristone's FDA-approved limit of 10 weeks.

HAWLEY INTRODUCES BILL TO STRIP FDA APPROVAL FROM 'INHERENTLY DANGEROUS' ABORTION PILL

Mize has led AUL for two-and-a-half years. The nonprofit has advocated against abortion, euthanasia, assisted suicide and other practices it considers threats to human life since its founding in 1971.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Mize said he believes Overton is the "right candidate" to lead the FDA, citing her experience in government, clinical medicine and medical research. If confirmed, Overton would take the reins of the agency responsible for regulating abortion medication, including mifepristone.

Mifepristone carries an FDA boxed warning, the agency’s strongest safety warning, for the risk of serious and sometimes fatal infections or bleeding.

Prompted initially by COVID-19 pandemic restrictions, the FDA stopped enforcing the drug's in-person dispensing requirement in 2021 and later removed it permanently after reviewing the available safety data.

Under current FDA rules, patients do not necessarily have to see a physician in person before receiving a prescription, allowing mifepristone to be prescribed after telehealth visit and mailed by a certified pharmacy. Mize wants those rules tightened.

SUPREME COURT TEMPORARILY BLOCKS APPEALS COURT RULING ON ABORTION PILL, RESTORES WIDER ACCESS TO DRUG

"Dr. Overton and I share a very similar perspective that the drug is dangerous, particularly in an unregulated way for women," Mize told Fox News Digital. "I firmly believe she understands the clinical implications of taking a drug with a black box warning and now shipping it in the mail."

Overton has publicly criticized mifepristone and other abortion drugs, which accounted for about 65% of clinician-provided abortions in 2023, according to the Guttmacher Institute, up from 53% in 2020 before the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade.

In a February 2023 policy brief for the America First Policy Institute, a MAGA-aligned think tank where she previously served as chief policy officer, Overton denounced federal policymakers for expanding access to abortion pills.

She also accused the Biden administration of using the COVID-19 pandemic to wrongly justify allowing mifepristone and misoprostol, a drug that induces early labor, to be sent to patients through the mail.

FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS

Taken together, the two drugs terminate early pregnancies: mifepristone blocks progesterone, a hormone needed to sustain the pregnancy, while misoprostol causes contractions that expel the fetus.

"Abortion is corrosive to children, women, and society broadly because it devalues and extinguishes innocent human life," she wrote at the time. "America First policies should focus on immediately halting the effort to normalize abortion-on-demand and on broadly recognizing the evidence of the risk posed to women."

Mize pointed to a 2025 study by the Ethics and Public Policy Center, a conservative think tank, that analyzed insurance claims from 865,727 mifepristone abortions between 2017 and 2023 and found a serious adverse event rate of nearly 11%. This included conditions such as hemorrhaging, sepsis or infection.

The study received immediate pushback, with the medical community saying it used a flawed methodology. The paper was also not peer-reviewed or published in a medical journal, factors Mize said Overton is aware of.

HAWLEY SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF 'LEFT-WING DARK-MONEY' GROUP OVER MAILED ABORTION DRUGS

"It's not the whole picture, and Dr. Overton would say that," Mize said. "But it's an important indicator as to what's happening in the real world. So I believe she will do a really good job of evaluating the study."

Mize said he hopes Overton will impose tighter restrictions on mifepristone after reviewing the evidence, potentially restoring a requirement that women see a doctor in person before receiving a prescription.

He described Overton as "measured" and "methodical" while cautioning that pro-life advocates should not expect her to pursue immediate, sweeping changes at the FDA.

"I don't get the sense that she's gonna move quickly on issues," Mize said.

SUPREME COURT KEEPS BROADER ACCESS TO ABORTION PILL MIFEPRISTONE IN PLACE WHILE LEGAL FIGHT CONTINUES

Dr. Marty Makary, the previous FDA commissioner, resigned in May after clashing with Trump administration officials and Republican lawmakers. He also drew criticism from pro-life activists, who accused the agency under his leadership of slow-walking its safety review of mifepristone.

If confirmed, Overton would inherit the review, which was formally announced in September 2025 and does not have a scheduled completion date. The FDA has noted these types of studies typically take a year or longer to conduct.

After that review is completed, Mize said the next step for Overton, ideally, would be "a longer term, deep dive evaluation on this medication to determine if it should even be on the market."

Mize acknowledged that not all the evidence is in yet but made clear that his preference would be to take mifepristone off the market.

"From my perspective, any medication that denies someone the opportunity to live and kills a human being shouldn't be something that we're promoting amongst the FDA," Mize said. "Ultimately, I would love to see this drug removed from the market for those reasons. Culturally, we might not be there right now."

Overton’s confirmation hearing has not yet been scheduled but is expected to take place after the Senate returns from its summer recess on Sept. 14.

item.title: DOJ sues to stop Ohio court blocking courthouse arrests
item.description: The Justice Department sued Franklin County Municipal Court over a rule blocking ICE civil arrests without a judicial warrant, citing federal law.
item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department sued an Ohio court Tuesday over a new rule blocking federal immigration arrests at or near the courthouse, accusing local officials of unlawfully interfering with federal enforcement and forcing ICE agents to make arrests in potentially riskier settings.

At issue is a Franklin County Municipal Court rule, which bars civil arrests at the courthouse unless officers have a judicial warrant. The DOJ argues the rule conflicts with federal immigration law, which allows ICE agents in certain circumstances to make arrests with administrative warrants or no warrant at all.

"This type of rule obstructs federal law enforcement and facilitates evasion of federal law by dangerous criminal aliens, despite Congress’s direction that federal agents detain and remove them," said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. "Throughout the country, and including in this courthouse specifically, federal agents have routinely and safely conducted arrests. The Department of Justice is committed to protecting that important federal prerogative."

JUDGE BLOCKS PHILADELPHIA LAW TARGETING MASKED FEDERAL OFFICERS

Those arrests can be less predictable and more dangerous because they may take place at homes, workplaces or other public locations, according to the complaint.

Two Columbus ICE officers have been hospitalized after encountering violence during at-large arrests in the past three months, DOJ says. The complaint does not identify the officers or provide details about the incidents.

ICE has also had to conduct longer surveillance and field operations to find people away from the courthouse. The DOJ says an arrest at a jail or courthouse may require two officers, while an arrest in the field typically requires four to six.

The department says courthouses offer a safer, more controlled setting because people entering are generally screened for weapons and other contraband. ICE agents have also coordinated with courthouse security and generally waited until hearings ended before making arrests, according to the complaint.

ICE made at least 12 arrests at Franklin County Municipal Court in recent years before the rule was adopted, DOJ says.

Rule 2.10 prohibits civil arrests of people at the courthouse for a proceeding or other lawful court business, but makes an exception for arrests carried out with a warrant issued by a judge.

The court began discussing changes in January amid pressure to prevent ICE from making civil arrests there, according to the complaint. The proposed rule was published for public comment in March and later adopted.

The rule says "the administration of justice … cannot be impeded by the other branches of the government" and that it should not be interpreted to violate the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause or federal immigration law.

DOJ argues it does both.

Federal immigration law allows ICE agents to make certain arrests using administrative warrants issued by federal immigration officials rather than judges. Agents can also make warrantless arrests in some circumstances, including when they have reason to believe someone is in the country illegally and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

DOJ says the Ohio court cannot impose a judicial-warrant requirement where federal law does not require one.

The lawsuit argues the rule violates the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause by improperly regulating the federal government and conflicting with federal immigration law.

DOJ is asking a federal judge to declare Rule 2.10 unlawful and block the court from enforcing it against federal officers.

The lawsuit names Franklin County Municipal Court, Administrative and Presiding Judge Jessica D’Varga and court security director Enoch White as defendants in their official capacities.
